title: Nutrients: what food is made of, and what each part does

summary.text: Pour lemon juice into hot milk, and it splits into white lumps and a pale, watery liquid. Milk was never one thing. Like almost every food, it is a mix of nutrients: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water. Each nutrient does a different job in your body. Food groups sort foods by the nutrient they give most, but most foods carry several.
summary.art: A steel tumbler of milk splitting into two parts: white curds in a cloth on one side and a pale yellow-green liquid in a glass on the other, with small labels around them: protein, fat, water, milk sugar, minerals.

intro.hook: Your school chart puts dal in the 'protein' box. But if you could pull apart a spoon of dry toor dal, more than half of it would be carbohydrate. So what is a 'protein food'? And what is inside the food we eat?
intro.text: Every food is made of a few kinds of nutrients. A nutrient is a part of food that your body uses to live, grow and move. In this unit you split milk into its parts, dry vegetables to find their water, and look for minerals hiding in clear water. Then you will know what the food group boxes really mean.
intro.art: A child at a kitchen table holding a spoon of yellow toor dal up to their eye, with a small chart behind them showing boxes labelled carbohydrate, protein, fat, vitamins, minerals and water.

outcomes: I can name the six kinds of nutrients and say one job each does in my body.
I can sort foods into food groups, and explain why many foods fit in more than one group.
I can split milk into curds and whey with lemon juice, and say which nutrients go where.
I can explain why my body needs water, and show that many foods are mostly water.
I can find signs of minerals in water and food, and name foods rich in calcium and iron.
I can tell how Fick and Wislicenus showed that muscles run mainly on carbohydrates and fats, not protein.

terms.meaning: A part of food that the body uses to live, grow, move and mend itself. There are six kinds: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.
terms.example: A glass of milk carries five kinds of nutrient at once: water, protein, fat, milk sugar and minerals, plus some vitamins.
terms.art: Six small jars on a shelf labelled carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.

terms.meaning: A box we sort foods into, by the nutrient they give most or the job they mostly do. Different books use different boxes.
terms.example: Rice goes in the carbohydrate group, because most of a grain of rice is starch.
terms.art: Five baskets labelled with food groups, with rice, dal, milk, ghee and fruit going into them.

terms.meaning: The nutrient your body uses most for energy. Sugars, starch and fibre are all carbohydrates.
terms.example: Idli, rice, ragi, chapati and banana are rich in carbohydrates.
terms.art: A plate of idli, a heap of rice and a banana, with a small flame drawn above them for energy.

terms.meaning: A carbohydrate made of many sugar pieces joined in a long chain. Plants store food as starch.
terms.example: Rice, potato and atta are mostly starch. Chew rice for a long time and it starts to taste a little sweet, as your spit breaks the starch into sugar.
terms.art: A long chain of small beads, with one bead breaking off as a sugar.

terms.meaning: A carbohydrate from plants that your body does not break down. It keeps food moving through your gut, and many of your gut microbes feed on it.
terms.example: Whole dal, green vegetables, fruit with its skin and whole grains have lots of fibre.
terms.art: A guava cut open, with its skin and seeds, next to a bowl of keerai.

terms.meaning: The nutrient your body uses to build and mend itself. Your muscles, hair, nails and skin are made mostly of protein.
terms.example: Dal, milk, curd, paneer, eggs, fish, peanuts and chana all give protein.
terms.art: A child flexing an arm, with a bowl of dal and a cube of paneer beside them.

terms.meaning: One of the small pieces that a protein is built from. There are 20 kinds, joined in long chains.
terms.example: Your body breaks the protein in dal into amino acids. Then it joins them again into your own proteins.
terms.art: A chain of 20 different coloured beads, being taken apart and joined in a new order.

terms.meaning: A nutrient that stores a lot of energy. It also builds the thin skin around every cell and helps the body take in some vitamins.
terms.example: Ghee, coconut oil, groundnut oil, peanuts and coconut are rich in fat.
terms.art: A small bowl of ghee, a coconut cut in half and a handful of peanuts.

terms.meaning: A nutrient the body needs in very small amounts to stay healthy. Each vitamin has its own jobs. They are named by letters: A, B, C, D, E and K.
terms.example: Amla and guava have lots of vitamin C, which helps cuts heal.
terms.art: An amla, a guava, a carrot and a mango, each with a small letter tag: C, C, A, A.

terms.meaning: A nutrient that comes from rocks and soil, through plants, animals and water. The body needs small amounts. Calcium, iron and iodine are minerals.
terms.example: The white rings that dry on a steel tumbler after you drink tap water are minerals left behind.
terms.art: A shiny steel tumbler with a white ring at the bottom, seen close up.

terms.meaning: A mineral that makes bones and teeth hard.
terms.example: Ragi, milk, curd, til and green leaves give calcium.
terms.art: A bowl of ragi kanji, a glass of milk and a small heap of til, next to a drawing of a bone.

terms.meaning: A mineral that your blood uses to carry oxygen around the body.
terms.example: Green leafy vegetables, dal, ragi, eggs, fish and meat give iron.
terms.art: A drop of red blood with tiny oxygen bubbles held in it, next to a bunch of keerai.

terms.meaning: When milk splits into soft white lumps and a watery liquid. An acid, like lemon juice, makes milk curdle.
terms.example: Lemon juice stirred into hot milk curdles it. This is how paneer is made.
terms.art: A spoon stirring lemon juice into a pan of milk, white lumps forming.

terms.meaning: When milk curdles, the white lumps are the curds. The pale, watery liquid left behind is the whey.
terms.example: Strain curdled milk through a cotton cloth. The curds stay in the cloth and become paneer. The whey drips through.
terms.art: A white cloth tied into a bundle of curds, dripping pale yellow whey into a bowl.

terms.meaning: What your body uses to move, think, grow and keep warm. Your body gets it from carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
terms.example: Running round the terrace uses energy that came from the idli you ate for breakfast.
terms.art: A child running on a terrace, with a faint idli drawn in a thought bubble.

terms.meaning: When the body has lost more water than it has taken in. You may feel thirsty, tired, or get a headache.
terms.example: After playing in the hot sun without drinking, you can become dehydrated.
terms.art: A tired child under a hot sun reaching for a tumbler of water.

explanations.definition: A nutrient is a part of food that the body uses to live, grow, move and mend itself. Scientists sort nutrients into six kinds: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.
explanations.description: Your body takes food apart into its nutrients. It burns some of them for energy. It uses others to build new parts, like muscle, bone and blood. Your body needs large amounts of carbohydrates, proteins, fats and water every day. It needs only tiny amounts of vitamins and minerals, but it cannot stay healthy without them.
examples: A plate of curd rice gives carbohydrate from the rice, and protein, fat, calcium and water from the curd.
A guava gives water, sugar, fibre and a lot of vitamin C.
explanations.art: A plate of curd rice with six small arrows coming out of it, each labelled with one nutrient.
explanations.context: This card explains what a nutrient is, and the six kinds of nutrient.

explanations.concept: Food groups: boxes to sort food
explanations.definition: A food group is a box of foods that give mostly the same nutrient, or do mostly the same job in the body.
explanations.description: Food groups help families plan meals. Different books use different boxes. Many Indian school books use three: energy-giving foods, body-building foods and protective foods. The Cambridge book uses five: carbohydrates, fruit and vegetables, protein, dairy, and fats and sugars. All of these are ways of sorting. A food is put in the box of the nutrient it gives most, or that it is best known for. But most foods carry several nutrients, so one food can belong in two or three boxes.
examples: Milk is in the dairy group. It also gives protein, fat and calcium, so it could go in the protein box too.
Peanuts are often called a protein food. But more than a third of a peanut is fat.
explanations.art: Five baskets labelled carbohydrates, fruit and vegetables, protein, dairy, and fats and sugars, with a bowl of dal balanced on the edge between two of them.
explanations.context: This card explains what food groups are, and why one food can fit in more than one group.

explanations.concept: Most foods are a mix of nutrients
explanations.definition: Almost every food from a plant or an animal contains several nutrients at once. Only a few, like sugar, salt and oil, are nearly one nutrient.
explanations.description: Scientists find out what is in a food by taking it apart in a laboratory. In India, the National Institute of Nutrition in Hyderabad has done this for hundreds of Indian foods. Their numbers surprise most people. Dry toor dal is about one-fifth protein, but more than half carbohydrate. Cooked rice is about two-thirds water. Milk is almost nine-tenths water. A cucumber is nearly all water.
examples: Out of every 10 spoons of dry toor dal: about 6 spoons carbohydrate, 2 protein, 1 fibre and 1 water.
Out of every 10 spoons of milk: about 9 spoons water. The last spoon is shared by milk sugar, fat, protein and minerals.
explanations.art: Two rows of ten spoons: one row for toor dal, coloured six yellow, two red, one green and one blue; one row for milk, nine blue and one striped.
explanations.context: This card shows that most foods carry several nutrients at once, with numbers for everyday Indian foods.

explanations.definition: Carbohydrates are sugars, starch and fibre. Your body breaks starch and sugars down into a sugar called glucose, and burns glucose for energy.
explanations.description: Starch is a long chain of sugar pieces joined together. Plants make starch to store food in their grains, roots and seeds. When you eat idli or rice, your body cuts the chain back into sugar. Your blood carries this sugar to every cell. Your brain runs mostly on glucose. Fibre is a carbohydrate too, but your body does not break it down. It keeps food moving through your gut, and many of the microbes living there feed on it.
examples: A runner eats rice or bananas before a race, because they give energy quickly.
Ragi, rice, wheat, millets, potatoes and sweet potatoes are all rich in starch.
explanations.art: A grain of rice opened up to show a long chain of beads inside, with a few beads breaking off and floating into a drop of blood.
explanations.context: This card explains carbohydrates, the nutrient the body uses most for energy.

explanations.concept: Proteins: building and mending the body
explanations.definition: Proteins are long chains of small pieces called amino acids. Your body uses them to build and mend itself.
explanations.description: Your muscles, skin, hair and nails are made mostly of protein. So are the tiny workers inside every cell that break food down. When you eat dal or curd, your body takes their proteins apart into amino acids. Then it joins those amino acids into its own proteins. Children need protein every day, because they are growing. In milk, most of the protein is one called casein. When milk becomes acidic, casein clumps together. That is why lemon juice makes milk curdle.
examples: When you scrape your knee, new skin grows over it. That new skin is built from protein.
Rice and dal eaten together give a better mix of amino acids than either one alone.
explanations.art: A chain of coloured beads being unpicked from a bowl of dal and rebuilt into the shape of a strong arm.
explanations.context: This card explains proteins, the nutrient the body uses to build and mend itself.

explanations.concept: Fats: stored energy and the skin of every cell
explanations.definition: Fats are nutrients that store a lot of energy. A spoon of fat gives about twice as much energy as a spoon of sugar or starch.
explanations.description: Your body stores spare energy as fat, under the skin and around the organs. Fat also builds the thin skin around every cell. And some vitamins, A, D, E and K, mix into fat and not into water. So the body takes them in better when a meal has a little fat. Fats that are liquid at room temperature are called oils.
examples: A carrot poriyal cooked in a little coconut oil helps your body take in the carrot's vitamin A.
Ghee and coconut oil go solid on a cold morning and melt on a hot day.
explanations.art: A small steel bowl of ghee and a bottle of coconut oil next to a drawing of a round cell with a thin outer skin.
explanations.context: This card explains fats: how they store energy and help build every cell.

explanations.definition: Vitamins are nutrients the body needs only in tiny amounts. Each one has its own jobs, and missing one for a long time makes a person ill.
explanations.description: Vitamin A helps your eyes see in dim light. It is in carrots, mangoes, papaya and green leaves. The B vitamins help your cells get energy out of food. They are in whole grains, dal, milk and eggs. Vitamin C helps cuts heal and keeps gums healthy. It is in amla, guava, lemon and oranges. Vitamin D helps your body use calcium. Your skin makes it when sunlight falls on it.
examples: Whey, the liquid left when you make paneer, is pale yellow-green partly because of vitamin B2 from the milk.
Ten to twenty minutes of play in the morning sun helps your skin make vitamin D.
explanations.art: A row of foods with vitamin letters: a carrot and a mango (A), a bowl of dal (B), an amla (C), and a child playing in sunlight (D).
explanations.context: This card explains vitamins, and what some of them do.

explanations.concept: Minerals: from rocks to your bones
explanations.definition: Minerals are nutrients that come from rocks and soil. Plants take them up from the soil with water. We get them from plants, from animals that ate plants, and from water.
explanations.description: Calcium makes bones and teeth hard. Ragi, milk, curd, til and green leaves give calcium. Iron is used by blood to carry oxygen. Green leaves, dal, ragi, eggs and fish give iron. Iodine helps the body grow and the brain develop. India adds iodine to most salt for this reason. Many minerals dissolve in water. That is why tap water can leave white rings when it dries on a steel tumbler.
examples: 100 grams of ragi flour has nearly three times as much calcium as 100 millilitres of milk.
Iron from green leaves is taken in better when the meal also has vitamin C, like a squeeze of lemon.
explanations.art: A plant's roots in soil with tiny coloured dots climbing up into the leaves, and a child eating those leaves, the same dots drawn in their bones.
explanations.context: This card explains minerals, where they come from and what some of them do.

explanations.concept: Water: the nutrient you need most of
explanations.definition: Water is a nutrient. More than half of your body is water, and you need more of it each day than any other nutrient.
explanations.description: Your blood is mostly water. It carries food and oxygen to your cells. Water in sweat cools you on a hot day. Water carries waste out of your body in urine. You lose water all day, in your breath, sweat and urine, so you must keep putting it back. A person can live for weeks without food, but only a few days without water. Much of your water comes from food. Rasam, curd rice, buttermilk, watermelon and cucumber are mostly water.
examples: Breathe onto a cold steel tumbler. The mist that forms is water from your own body.
Pale yellow urine usually means you have had enough to drink. Dark yellow means drink more.
explanations.art: A child breathing a patch of mist onto a cold steel tumbler, with a jug of water and a slice of watermelon on the table.
explanations.context: This card explains why water is a nutrient, and how the body uses and loses it.

explanations.description: For about 40 years, many doctors told people to eat as little fat as possible, to keep their hearts healthy. Today most scientists agree the body needs some fat, and the kind of fat matters. They still argue about some fats, like ghee and coconut oil. Most agree that trans fats, found in some reused frying oils and some packaged snacks, are harmful.
examples: Peanuts, til and fish give fats that most scientists agree are good for the heart.
Oil used again and again for frying pakoras can form harmful fats.

perspectives.who: Many heart doctors and health guidelines
perspectives.explanation: Eat some fat, mostly from plant oils, nuts, seeds and fish. Keep ghee, butter and coconut oil to small amounts, because they may raise the kind of fat in the blood that clogs arteries.
The evidence against ghee and coconut oil is weaker than people think. What matters more is the whole diet: too much sugar and too many fried, packaged foods.

explanations.art: A doctor and a scientist at a table, looking at a small bowl of ghee and a bottle of groundnut oil, with question marks between them.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: how much fat, and which fats, are good for us.

agreed.text: The body needs six kinds of nutrient: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.
agreed.evidence: When people go without one of them for a long time, they fall ill in a way that is typical for that nutrient. Without vitamin C, gums bleed. Without iodine, the neck can swell. Giving back the missing nutrient makes them well.

agreed.text: Most foods contain several nutrients at once.
agreed.evidence: Food scientists have taken thousands of foods apart in laboratories and measured what is in them. In India, the National Institute of Nutrition in Hyderabad publishes these numbers for Indian foods.

agreed.text: Muscles get most of their energy from carbohydrates and fats. Protein is used mostly to build and mend the body.
agreed.evidence: In 1865, Fick and Wislicenus measured how much protein their bodies broke down while climbing a mountain. It was far too little to give the energy they used. Many experiments since then agree.

agreed.text: Proteins are built from amino acids, and the body builds its own proteins from the amino acids in food.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can follow labelled amino acids from a meal into the proteins of muscle and blood.

agreed.text: Milk curdles when it becomes acidic, because its main protein, casein, clumps together.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can see it at home with lemon juice. Dairy scientists measure the exact acidity at which casein clumps.

challenging.claim: Dal is a protein food, so it is mostly protein.
challenging.who: A common idea, from food group charts
challenging.for: Dal is one of the best sources of protein for vegetarian families. It has much more protein than rice or wheat.
challenging.against: Measured in a laboratory, dry toor dal is about one-fifth protein and more than half carbohydrate. It is in the protein box because it gives more protein than most plant foods, not because it is mostly protein.
challenging.context: This card looks at what it means to call dal a protein food.

challenging.claim: Muscles burn their own protein to do work, so hard workers need mostly protein.
challenging.who: Justus von Liebig, a famous German chemist, in the 1840s
challenging.for: Muscles are made of protein, so it seemed natural that working muscles use up protein.
challenging.against: Fick and Wislicenus climbed a mountain in 1865 and measured the protein their bodies broke down. It could supply only a small part of the energy they used. The rest came from carbohydrates and fats.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of a famous scientist, and how it was tested.

challenging.claim: Water is not food, so it is not a nutrient.
challenging.for: Water has no energy in it and does not fill you up like a meal.
challenging.against: Your body uses water in every cell, in blood, sweat and urine. You need more of it each day than any other nutrient, and you would fall ill within days without it. So scientists count it as a nutrient.
challenging.context: This card asks whether water should count as a nutrient.

challenging.claim: Whey is waste and should be thrown away after making paneer.
challenging.for: The paneer is what you wanted. The whey looks thin and watery.
challenging.against: Whey holds milk sugar, minerals, some vitamins and a little protein. Many cooks use it to knead chapati dough or to cook dal or rice.
challenging.context: This card is about the pale liquid left after making paneer.

challenging.claim: The more vitamins you take, the healthier you are.
challenging.for: Vitamins are needed for health, and a child short of a vitamin does get better with more of it.
challenging.against: The body needs only small amounts. Most children who eat a mix of foods get enough. Too much of some vitamins, like A and D, can make a person ill. Doctors give vitamin tablets when a test shows a child needs them.
challenging.context: This card looks at the idea that more vitamins is always better.

big_questions.q: When you drink milk, its protein is taken apart and built into your muscles. At what moment does the milk stop being milk and start being you?
big_questions.hint: Think of each step: in the glass, in your stomach, in your blood, in your muscle. Is there one moment, or does it change slowly?

big_questions.q: Sugar, oil and paneer look and taste completely different. Yet they are made mostly of the same three kinds of atoms. How can that be?
big_questions.hint: Think of how the same few letters make very different words, depending on their order.

big_questions.q: A calf lives on milk alone for weeks. Why can a calf do that, but a child of eight cannot?
big_questions.hint: What is in milk, and what is missing? Think of iron and vitamin C. What does a calf start eating as they grow?

big_questions.q: We sort foods into boxes, but most foods belong in several. Are food groups real, or only a useful habit?
big_questions.hint: Who made the boxes, and why? Would a bee or a cow sort foods into the same boxes?

big_questions.q: A plant takes calcium from rocks in the soil. You eat the plant, and the calcium becomes your bones. Where did your bones come from, really?
big_questions.hint: Follow the calcium back: bone, ragi, soil, rock. Where did the rock get it?

big_questions.q: Why does the body need tiny amounts of so many different vitamins, instead of one big helper?
big_questions.hint: Each vitamin helps a different job in the cell. Nobody knows a full answer to why life uses so many.

story.title: The Green-Yellow Water
story.note: Kavya, her aunt and her brother are made up. The science is true: lemon juice curdles hot milk, the curds hold most of the protein and fat, and whey is mostly water with milk sugar, minerals and some vitamins. Its yellow-green colour comes partly from vitamin B2 (riboflavin).
text: Kavya was nine, and she lived in Madurai, in a flat on the third floor. On Friday her teacher gave the class a job for the weekend. 'Make a food group chart,' she said. 'Draw five boxes. Put ten foods in the right boxes.'

On Saturday morning Kavya sat at the dining table with a big sheet of paper. She drew five boxes: carbohydrates, fruit and vegetables, protein, dairy, and fats and sugars. Her little brother Arjun, who was six, watched her and ate a banana.

'Rice goes in carbohydrates,' Kavya said, and drew a heap of rice. 'Banana goes in fruit.' Arjun held up his banana skin. 'Dal goes in protein. Ghee goes in fats.' She drew a glass of milk in the dairy box and sat back. Ten foods, five boxes. It was easy.

Her aunt, Revathi Athai, came in from the kitchen. Athai worked in a laboratory at a big dairy, where she tested milk all day. She was staying with them for Arjun's birthday, and she was making paneer for the birthday dinner.
Athai looked at the chart for a long time. 'Very neat,' she said. 'But I have a question. Why is the milk only in the dairy box?'
'Because milk is dairy,' said Kavya. 'Dairy means things made from milk.'
'True,' said Athai. 'But what is milk made of? Come and see.'

In the kitchen a big pan of milk was on the stove. Small bubbles were forming at the edges, and steam was rising. Athai turned off the flame. She squeezed two lemons into a small cup. 'Stand back a little, because the milk is very hot,' she said. Then she poured the lemon juice into the pan and stirred gently with a big spoon.

Kavya watched. For a moment nothing happened. Then soft white lumps began to form, all through the milk. They grew bigger and joined together. Around them, the milk was turning into a thin, clear liquid. It was not white any more. It was a pale green-yellow.
'Where did the milk go?' asked Arjun, who had come to watch.

'It is all still here,' said Athai. 'It has only split into two parts.' She laid a thin cotton cloth over a steel strainer, set it on a big bowl and poured the pan out. The white lumps stayed in the cloth. The green-yellow liquid ran through into the bowl.

'The lumps are called curds,' said Athai. 'They hold most of the milk's protein, with most of its fat caught inside, and some water. When I press them, they become paneer. The liquid is called whey. It is mostly water, but it also carries the milk's sugar, some minerals and some vitamins. One of those vitamins, B2, is part of why it looks green-yellow.'
Kavya looked into the bowl. There was much more whey than curd. 'So milk is mostly water?'

'Almost nine-tenths water,' said Athai. 'The other tenth is protein, fat, milk sugar and minerals, all mixed up so finely that the milk looks like one thing. The lemon juice made the protein clump together, so now we can see them apart.'

Kavya picked up the bowl of whey to pour it into the sink. 'Wait!' said Athai. 'That is not waste. Let me show you.' She took a clean steel plate, dropped two spoons of whey onto it and put it on the balcony in the sun. 'Look at it tomorrow,' she said.
That afternoon Athai kneaded the chapati dough with whey instead of water. At dinner, Arjun ate four chapatis and three pieces of paneer, and said it was the best birthday food ever.

On Sunday morning Kavya ran to the balcony. The whey on the plate had dried. The water had gone into the air. Left behind was a thin, sticky, yellowish film. She touched it with a finger. It was a little sticky, like the inside of a sweet wrapper.
'That is the milk sugar and the minerals,' said Athai. 'The water went into the air, and they stayed.'

Kavya went back to her chart. She looked at the glass of milk in the dairy box. Then she drew a dotted line from the milk to the protein box, and another to the fats box. She wrote next to it: 'Milk is mostly water. It also has protein, fat, milk sugar and minerals.'
Then she looked at the dal. 'Athai, is dal only protein?'
Athai smiled. 'What do you think? We could look it up in the book of Indian foods.'
They looked it up together. Dry toor dal was about one-fifth protein, and more than half carbohydrate. Kavya drew another dotted line, from the dal to the carbohydrate box.

By lunchtime her chart had dotted lines going everywhere. Peanuts went to protein and fats. Ragi went to carbohydrates, and had a note: 'lots of calcium'. Curd went to dairy, protein and fats. Arjun looked at it and frowned. 'It is messy now.'

'It is true now,' said Kavya. 'A box only says what a food gives the most. It does not say everything that is in it.' She showed Arjun the dried whey on the plate. 'See? Milk has lots of things hiding in it. You only see them when you split it apart.'
Arjun licked his finger, touched the sticky film and tasted it. 'Sweet,' he said. 'A little bit.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: a food group names the nutrient a food is best known for, but almost every food is a mix. Splitting milk with lemon juice shows this. The curds hold most of the protein and fat, and the whey holds water, milk sugar, minerals and some vitamins.
ask: Why did the milk split into two parts when Athai poured in the lemon juice?
What did Athai say the curds were mostly made of? And the whey?
What was left on the plate when the whey dried in the sun? Where had the water gone?
Why did Kavya draw dotted lines on her chart? Do you think the chart was better or worse afterwards?
Which food in your kitchen would you like to split apart, to see what is inside?

games.title: Two-Box Foods: a sorting card game

printables.title: A mat with five boxes: carbohydrates, fruit and vegetables, protein, dairy, fats and sugars
items: Draw five big boxes on a sheet of paper and write one food group in each.

printables.title: Points sheet
items: 1 point: a food in its usual box
2 more points: a second box for the same food, with a true reason

Answer card for the parent: Toor dal (protein and carbohydrates), Peanuts (protein and fats), Milk (dairy, protein and fats), Curd (dairy and protein), Paneer (dairy, protein and fats), Coconut (fats, and fruit), Til laddoo (fats and sugars, with calcium), Ragi mudde (carbohydrates, with calcium), Banana (fruit and carbohydrates), Egg (protein and fats)

rules: Shuffle the food cards and put them face down.
On your turn, take a card and put it in the box where it usually goes. That scores 1 point.
If you think the food also belongs in a second box, say which, and give a reason. For example: 'Peanuts go in protein, but they are also more than a third fat.'
The other players check the answer card. A true reason scores 2 more points. Lay the card across the two boxes.
Play until the cards run out. The highest score wins.
Playing alone: try to find a second box for at least 8 foods.

flow.do: 1. Draw the five-box mat. 2. Cut out the 20 food cards. 3. Shuffle them face down.
flow.say: Every food has a usual box. But many foods carry more than one nutrient. Today you score extra for finding a second box.
flow.kid: Put the food cards face down. Each food has a usual box. Can you find a second box too?
flow.context: This is the first step of Two-Box Foods. It is a card game where you sort foods into food groups and score extra for foods that fit two groups.

flow.do: Take turns. Check each second-box reason against the answer card.
flow.say: Toor dal. Its usual box is protein. Is there a second box? Why?
flow.kid: Take a card. Put it in its usual box. Can it go in a second box? Say why.

check.q: Toor dal is in the protein box. Which second box is true for dal?
options: Carbohydrates, because more than half of dry dal is carbohydrate
Fats and sugars, because dal is oily
Dairy, because dal is cooked with milk
check.why: More than half of dry toor dal is carbohydrate, mostly starch. Dal has very little fat, and it is not made from milk. Ghee added at the table brings fat, but that comes from the ghee.

flow.do: At the end, count the cards lying across two boxes.
flow.say: Look how many foods lie across two boxes. What does that tell you about food groups?
flow.kid: Count the cards lying across two boxes. What does that tell you?
flow.parent: A good answer: food groups say what a food gives most, but most foods give several nutrients.

flow.kid: Each card shows a food split into 10 spoons. Blue is water. Yellow is carbohydrate. Red is protein. Orange is fat. Match the foods.

flow.kid: Take a food card. Put it on a spoon card. Say why.

check.why: White sugar is almost all carbohydrate, so all 10 spoons are yellow. Sugar and oil are rare foods that are nearly one nutrient. Most foods are mixes.

flow.say: Which match was hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Check your answers. Which one was hardest?
flow.parent: Cucumber and milk are often mixed up, because both are mostly water. Banana and cooked rice are also close: both are mostly water and carbohydrate.

games.context: This is a matching game. You match foods to cards that show their mix of nutrients out of 10 spoons.

setup.art: Eight small cards in a row, each with ten coloured circles in different mixes of blue, yellow, red, orange and green.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the 8 spoon cards.

setup.art: A child placing a 'coconut oil' card on a spoon card with ten orange circles.
setup.caption: 2. Match each food to its spoon card and say why.

items.p: Which of these is a nutrient?
items.why: Protein is a part of food that your body uses to build and mend itself. A spoon and a plate hold food, but they are not part of it.

items.p: Match each nutrient to one job it does in your body.
pairs: gives energy to run and think
makes up most of your blood
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each nutrient has its own jobs. These are the main ones for each.

items.p: Sort these foods into the group they are best known for.
items.a: see items
items.why: Idli and rice are mostly starch. Dal and egg are known for protein. Ghee and coconut oil are nearly all fat.

items.p: Water is a nutrient.
items.why: True. Your body uses water in every cell, in blood, sweat and urine. You need more water each day than any other nutrient.

items.p: When lemon juice makes hot milk split, the white lumps are called ____ and the watery liquid is called ____.
items.why: The curds hold most of the milk's protein and fat. The whey is mostly water, with milk sugar and minerals.

items.p: Meena, a girl in Class 3, adds salt water to hot milk. Nothing happens. Then she adds lemon juice, and white lumps appear. Why?
opts: Lemon juice is an acid, and acid makes milk's protein clump
items.why: Lemon juice is sour, which means it is an acid. Acid makes casein, the main protein in milk, clump into curds. Salt water is not an acid, so the milk stays smooth.

items.p: After splitting milk with lemon juice, there was much more whey than curd. What does this tell you about milk?
items.a: Milk is mostly water. The water went into the whey. Only a small part of milk is protein and fat, which made the curds.
items.why: A strong answer joins what was seen (lots of whey) to what it means (milk is mostly water).

items.p: Label the parts in the drawing of milk being strained: curds, whey, cotton cloth, strainer.
items.why: The cloth sits in the strainer and catches the curds. The whey runs through into the bowl below.
items.art: A strainer lined with cloth on a bowl, white lumps in the cloth and pale liquid in the bowl, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Rice, ragi, potato, ghee.
items.a: ghee
items.why: Ghee is nearly all fat. Rice, ragi and potato are mostly starch, which is a carbohydrate.

items.p: Which mineral does your blood use to carry oxygen?
items.why: Iron is the mineral blood uses to carry oxygen. Green leafy vegetables, dal, ragi, eggs and fish give iron. Sugar is not a mineral.

items.p: Draw a plate of food you like. Next to each food, write the nutrient it gives most.
items.a: Any plate with each food labelled correctly. For example: rice, carbohydrate. Sambar, protein and water. Poriyal, vitamins and fibre. Curd, protein and calcium.
items.why: This shows the child can connect the foods they eat with the nutrients in them.

items.p: A cucumber is mostly water.
items.why: True. A cucumber is nearly all water. That is why a slice shrinks to a thin, wrinkly disc when it dries.

items.p: Why do you need to drink water every day, even on a day you sit still?
items.a: Water leaves my body all day, in my breath, sweat and urine. So I need to put it back.
items.why: A good answer names at least two ways water leaves the body.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, is making a food group chart. She has to decide where milk goes.

views.says: Milk goes in the dairy box. Dairy means food made from milk, and that is what the chart asks.
Milk should also go in the protein box and the fats box. It carries protein and fat, and mostly water.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you saw in the milk-splitting test. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence: lemon juice split milk into curds, which hold most of its protein and fat, and whey, which is mostly water. It also says what the other side has right: the dairy box is useful for planning meals, because milk foods all give calcium.
items.why: Both are right in a way. The boxes are a useful habit, but they name only part of what is inside a food.

items.p: The carbohydrate that plants use to store food, found in rice and potatoes, is called ____.
items.why: Starch is a long chain of sugar pieces joined together.

items.p: Put the steps of the milk-splitting test in order.
items: Pour it through a cotton cloth
A grown-up heats the milk and pours it into tumblers
Add 1 tablespoon of each liquid and stir
Wait 3 minutes and look for lumps
a: A grown-up heats the milk and pours it into tumblers
Add 1 tablespoon of each liquid and stir
Wait 3 minutes and look for lumps
Pour it through a cotton cloth
items.why: Heat, add, wait and look, then separate the curds from the whey.

items.p: Dry toor dal is about one-fifth protein and more than half carbohydrate. Why is it put in the protein group?
opts: It gives more protein than most plant foods
items.why: Dal has far more protein than rice or wheat, so it is a very useful protein food, especially for vegetarians. But most of it is carbohydrate. Picking 'mostly protein' is what the box makes people think.

items.p: Peanuts are often called a protein food. Using what you know, explain why a peanut could also go in the fats group.
items.a: More than a third of a peanut is fat, which is more than its protein. So it belongs in the fats group too.
items.why: A strong answer uses the numbers: more fat than protein in a peanut.

items.p: In the sun-dried slices test, a potato slice kept about a fifth of its weight. A cucumber slice kept almost nothing. Which had more of something that is not water?
opts: The potato, because it has a lot of starch
The cucumber, because it is green
Both the same, because they were the same size
items.why: What is left after drying is the part of a food that is not water. A potato keeps more because about a fifth of it is starch. A cucumber is nearly all water.

items.p: Tap water left a white ring when it dried on a steel plate. Filtered water left almost nothing. Explain why.
items.a: Tap water carries minerals like calcium, dissolved from rocks and soil. When the water dried, the minerals stayed. The filter took most minerals out.
items.why: A strong answer says the minerals were dissolved, so they could not be seen, and stayed behind when the water left.

items.p: Fibre is a carbohydrate that your body breaks down for energy.
items.why: False. Fibre is a carbohydrate, but your body does not break it down. It keeps food moving through your gut, and many gut microbes feed on it.

items.p: Match each vitamin to one job it does.
pairs: helps eyes see in dim light
help cells get energy from food
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each vitamin has its own jobs. These are well known ones.

items.p: Why does a carrot poriyal cooked in a little oil help your body more than a raw carrot alone?
opts: Vitamin A mixes into fat, so the body takes it in better with a little oil
items.why: Vitamins A, D, E and K mix into fat, not water. A little fat in the meal helps the body take them in.

items.p: A spoon of fat gives about twice as much energy as a spoon of sugar. Why might the body store spare energy as fat, not as sugar?
items.a: Fat holds more energy in the same amount, so it takes up less room in the body. It is a good way to keep energy for later.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that fat packs more energy into less space.

items.p: Sort these minerals and vitamins.
items.a: see items
items.why: Minerals come from rocks and soil. Vitamins are made by living things, or by your skin in sunlight for vitamin D.

items.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 4, wants to throw away the whey after his mother makes paneer.

views.says: It is just watery stuff. The paneer is the food we wanted.
Whey still carries milk sugar, minerals and some vitamins. We should knead the chapati dough with it.
It is mostly water, and it is sour. A little of it in dough is fine, but there is too much to use every time.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Use what you saw when whey dried on a plate. Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the dried whey: it left a sticky film of milk sugar and minerals, so whey is not empty. It can also agree with Nandini that a family may not use all of it, and suggest a plan like rasam or rice.
items.why: All three have a point: whey carries nutrients, it is mostly water, and using all of it takes planning.

items.p: Proteins are built from small pieces called ____ ____.
items.why: There are 20 kinds of amino acid. Your body breaks the protein in food into them, and builds its own proteins from them.

items.p: Label the body outline: muscles (protein), bones (calcium), blood (iron), eyes (vitamin A).
items.why: These are four places where a nutrient does one of its best-known jobs.
items.art: A simple outline of a child's body with four blank label lines pointing to an arm muscle, a leg bone, a blood vessel and an eye.

items.p: Iron from keerai is taken in better with a squeeze of lemon. Plan a lunch that does this, and explain why it works.
items.a: Keerai poriyal, rice and dal with a squeeze of lemon. The lemon gives vitamin C, which helps the body take in the iron from the keerai and dal.
items.why: A strong answer pairs an iron food with a vitamin C food and says why.

items.p: Put the journey of calcium in order, from the ground to your body.
items: Rocks slowly break down into soil
The ragi plant takes calcium up from the soil
Calcium is built into your bones
a: Rocks slowly break down into soil
The ragi plant takes calcium up from the soil
Calcium is built into your bones
items.why: Minerals start in rocks, reach plants through soil and water, and reach us through food.

items.p: Draw two tumblers of milk: one before lemon juice is added, one 3 minutes after. Label what you see in each.
items.a: Before: smooth white milk. After: white lumps (curds) in a thin pale yellow-green liquid (whey).
items.why: The drawing shows that one smooth liquid split into two parts.
items.art: Two empty tumbler outlines side by side.

items.p: Put the steps of the Faulhorn test by Fick and Wislicenus in order.
items: They measured the nitrogen in their urine
They ate no protein, only starch, fat and sugar
They worked out that protein gave only a small part of the energy
a: They ate no protein, only starch, fat and sugar
They measured the nitrogen in their urine
They worked out that protein gave only a small part of the energy
items.why: First they made sure no protein came from food. Then they climbed, measured the nitrogen, which comes from protein the body breaks down, and compared the energy.

items.p: Fick and Wislicenus ate only starch, fat and sugar before their climb. Why was this important for their test?
opts: So that any protein used would come from their own bodies, not from a meal
Because starch is lighter to carry
items.why: With no protein in their food, any nitrogen in their urine had to come from their body's own protein. That made the measurement clear.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether cold milk curdles with lemon juice as well as hot milk. Say what you would change, what you would keep the same, and what you would look at.
items.a: I would change only the temperature of the milk: one tumbler hot and one cold. I would keep the amount of milk, the amount of lemon juice, the stirring and the waiting time the same. I would look at how many lumps form and how big they are after 3 minutes.
items.why: A strong design changes one thing, keeps the rest the same, and says what will be compared.

items.p: Three people argue about the best way to describe dal.

views.says: Dry dal is more than half carbohydrate and about one-fifth protein.

views.who: A mother cooking for a vegetarian family
views.says: Dal is our protein. Without it, our meals would have very little protein.

items.ask: Which description is most useful, and for whom? Give a reason. Then answer back from one of the other points of view.
items.a: Any well-argued answer. For example: the scientist's description is most accurate, but the mother's is most useful for planning meals, because for her family dal gives more protein than any other food.
items.why: Each view is true for a different purpose. A strong answer says which purpose matters to them.

items.p: A calf lives on milk alone for weeks. Name two nutrients a child of eight would run short of on milk alone, and say where else they could get them.
items.a: Iron, because milk has very little iron: keerai, dal and ragi give it. Vitamin C, because milk has little: amla, guava and lemon give it. Fibre too: whole grains, dal and vegetables.
items.why: A strong answer names nutrients milk lacks, like iron, vitamin C and fibre, with foods that give them.

items.p: Sugar, oil and paneer look completely different. What are they mostly made of?
opts: The same three kinds of atoms, carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, joined in different ways
items.why: Sugar, fat and protein are all built mostly from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms. Protein also has nitrogen. How the atoms are joined makes each one so different.

items.p: Many people think that the more vitamin tablets a healthy child takes, the healthier the child becomes. True or false?
items.why: False. The body needs only tiny amounts of vitamins, and most children who eat a mix of foods get enough. Too much of some vitamins, like A and D, can make a person ill.

items.p: Your body can make a little vitamin D by itself, when sunlight falls on your skin.
items.why: True. Skin makes vitamin D in sunlight. Some foods, like eggs and fish, give vitamin D too.

items.p: Coconut water and whey both left a sticky film when they dried. Tap water left a white ring. What different things might each one be leaving behind?
items.a: The sticky film is mostly sugars, with some minerals. The white ring from tap water is mostly minerals like calcium, with no sugar.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the residue felt like, sticky or not, to tell sugar from minerals.

items.p: Match each finding to the person or group who made it.
pairs: said muscles burn their own protein
showed muscles run mainly on carbohydrates and fats
measures what is in Indian foods
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are the people and the institute named in this unit.

items.p: Ragi has nearly three times as much calcium as the same weight of milk. Why do you think most food charts put milk, not ragi, first for calcium?
items.a: Many charts were first made in countries where milk is the usual food and ragi is not eaten. Milk is also easy to drink every day. Charts may not include the grains that families in South India have eaten for a long time.
items.why: Good answers think about who made the chart and what foods they knew.

items.p: Draw a cycle that shows how the water in a cucumber could end up inside you, and then back in the air.
items.a: Rain falls on soil, the cucumber plant drinks the water, you eat the cucumber, the water goes into your blood, and you breathe or sweat it back into the air, where it forms clouds.
items.why: This joins water in food, water in the body and water leaving the body.
items.art: An empty circle with arrows going round it.

items.p: In the milk-splitting test, tamarind water made fewer lumps than lemon juice. What is the most likely reason?
opts: Tamarind water was less strongly acidic than the lemon juice
items.why: How quickly and fully milk curdles depends on how acidic the liquid is. Tamarind water is sour, but often less strongly than lemon juice. Adding more tamarind water usually gives more lumps.

items.p: When you drink milk, its protein is taken apart into amino acids and built into your muscle. Is that muscle still milk, or is it you? Explain what you think.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: the amino acids came from the milk, but they have been joined in a new way, so now they are part of me.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer uses the idea that amino acids are taken apart and joined again.

items.p: Sort these foods: is each one nearly a single nutrient, or a mix of many?
items.a: see items
items.why: Sugar is nearly all carbohydrate, oil nearly all fat, salt nearly all minerals. Most whole foods, like milk, dal and peanuts, are mixes.

experiments.title: Splitting Milk: which kitchen liquids curdle it?
experiments.question: Which liquids from our kitchen make hot milk split into curds and whey, and which do not?
experiments.predict: Look at the six cups of liquid: lemon juice, vinegar, tamarind water, salt water, sugar water and plain water. Which ones do you think will make milk split into lumps? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same amount of milk in every tumbler, half a cup, all from the same pan. Add the same amount of each liquid, 1 tablespoon. Stir each one the same way, five slow stirs, and wait the same time, 3 minutes. Only the liquid changes. Plain water is the comparison, so we can see what milk does with nothing special added.
results_table: My guess: will it curdle? (yes or no)
After 3 minutes: lumps? (none, a few, many)
Colour of the liquid around the lumps

materials.item: milk, any kind from a packet or a milkman (full-cream curdles into the biggest lumps)
6 steel tumblers or small steel bowls, all the same size
juice of 1 or 2 lemons
white vinegar, if you have it (skip this cup if not, or use sour curd instead)
tamarind water: a lemon-sized ball of tamarind soaked in 4 tablespoons of hot water for 10 minutes and squeezed
salt water: a big pinch of salt in 2 tablespoons of water
sugar water: a teaspoon of sugar in 2 tablespoons of water
plain drinking water
a tablespoon, a pan, paper slips and a pencil for labels
a thin cotton cloth (an old clean dupatta, veshti or handkerchief) and a tea strainer or steel strainer
a clear glass or a measuring cup, to look at the whey

experiments.safety: Hot milk can scald. A grown-up heats the milk and pours it. The child adds the liquids with a spoon only after the grown-up says the tumblers are cool enough to touch on the outside. Never taste vinegar straight from the bottle.

schedule.what: Guess which liquids will curdle milk. Add each liquid to hot milk, wait 3 minutes and look. Strain the lemon cup into curds and whey. Keep 2 spoons of whey for the mineral test.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the lemon tumbler after 3 minutes and label the curds and the whey. Then write: what I think, what I saw, and why.

flow.do: 1. Put the six tumblers in a row. 2. Put a paper label in front of each: lemon, vinegar, tamarind, salt, sugar, water. 3. Put 1 tablespoon of each liquid in a small cup beside its label.
flow.say: Milk looks like one smooth white liquid. Today we find out if it is really one thing. Look at these six liquids. Which ones do you think will make milk split into lumps? Why?
flow.kid: Put six tumblers in a row. Label them: lemon, vinegar, tamarind, salt, sugar, water. Which ones will make milk go lumpy? Guess. Say why.

ask.q: Why did you guess that one?
good: Lemon makes things sour, and sour things spoil milk.
Salt water is just water, so nothing will happen.
I have seen milk go lumpy when it goes bad.

flow.parent: Write down the guesses in the table before you start. Any guess with a reason is good. Many children think salt will curdle milk, because salt 'does things' in cooking. Don't correct the guesses now. The test will answer them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the milk-splitting experiment. You guess which kitchen liquids will make hot milk split into lumps.

flow.do: 1. Heat the milk in a pan until it steams and tiny bubbles form at the edge. Do not let it boil over. 2. Turn off the flame. 3. Pour half a cup into each of the six tumblers. 4. Wait 2 minutes for the tumblers to cool a little.
flow.say: I am heating the milk, because hot milk splits much faster than cold milk. Stay back from the stove while I pour.
flow.kid: A grown-up heats the milk and pours it. Stand back. Hot milk can burn you. Wait until they say it is safe.
flow.parent: Hot milk works best, about as hot as tea you would wait to sip. Cold milk also curdles with lemon juice, but slowly and with tiny lumps that are hard to see. Feel the outside of each tumbler before your child touches it.

flow.do: 1. Add 1 tablespoon of lemon juice to the lemon tumbler. 2. Stir slowly five times. 3. Do the same for each liquid in its own tumbler, with a rinsed spoon each time. 4. Start a 3-minute timer after the last one.
flow.say: Add one liquid to each tumbler. Five slow stirs. Rinse the spoon each time, so no lemon gets into the next cup.
flow.kid: Add one spoon of liquid to its tumbler. Stir five times, slowly. Rinse the spoon. Do the next one.
flow.parent: Rinsing the spoon matters. A drop of lemon in the sugar tumbler could start it curdling and spoil the test.

flow.do: 1. After 3 minutes, tilt each tumbler gently towards the light. 2. Look for white lumps, and for a thin, clear liquid around them. 3. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Tilt each tumbler and look closely. Do you see lumps? What colour is the liquid around them?
flow.kid: Tilt each tumbler gently. Do you see white lumps? Is the milk still smooth? Write what you see.

check.q: Lemon, vinegar and tamarind made the milk split into lumps. Salt, sugar and plain water did not. What do lemon, vinegar and tamarind have in common?
check.why: Lemon juice, vinegar and tamarind are all sour. Sour things are acids. An acid makes the main protein in milk, casein, clump together into lumps. Picking 'from plants' is a fair thought, but sugar comes from a plant too, and sugar water did not curdle the milk. Picking 'yellow' doesn't work, because vinegar is clear.

flow.parent: You should see thick white lumps and pale green-yellow liquid in the lemon and vinegar tumblers within a minute or two. Tamarind water usually curdles hot milk too, sometimes more slowly, with brownish whey. Salt, sugar and water tumblers stay smooth. If the lemon tumbler shows only tiny lumps, the milk was not hot enough. Add one more tablespoon of lemon juice and stir.

flow.do: 1. Lay the cotton cloth over the strainer and hold it over a clear glass. 2. Pour the lemon tumbler through it. 3. Gather the cloth and gently squeeze. 4. Compare how much is in the cloth and how much is in the glass.
flow.say: Let's separate the two parts. The cloth will catch the lumps. Which part do you think will be bigger?
flow.kid: Pour the lumpy milk through the cloth. The lumps stay. The liquid runs into the glass. Which part is bigger?
flow.parent: The white lumps are called curds. They hold most of the milk's protein and fat, with some water still inside. Pressed together, they are paneer. The pale liquid is whey. It is mostly water, with milk sugar, minerals and some vitamins. There will be much more whey than curd. Keep 2 spoons of whey in a small cup for the Hidden Minerals test (e3).

ask.q: Why is there so much more whey than curd?
good: Milk is mostly water, and the water went into the whey.
The lumps are only a small part of the milk.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then tell them what the curds and whey are made of.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now about milk? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: milk is not one thing, it is a mix of parts. What I saw: sour liquids made white lumps and a pale watery liquid, and salt, sugar and water did nothing. There was much more liquid than lumps. Why: the sour liquids made the protein in milk clump, so it came out of the water. After their answer, explain that the curds hold most of the milk's protein and fat, and the whey is mostly water, milk sugar and minerals. So milk, which we put in the dairy box, also gives protein, fat, water and minerals.

experiments.title: Sun-Dried Slices: how much of a vegetable is water?
experiments.question: Which foods lose the most when they dry in the sun: cucumber, tomato, potato, carrot or chapati? What does that tell us about the water in them?
experiments.predict: Put the five slices in order, from the one you think will shrink most to the one you think will shrink least. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Cut every slice the same thickness, about half a centimetre, and about the same size. Dry them all on the same plate, in the same place, for the same number of days. Only the food changes. If you have a kitchen scale, weigh each slice before and after, because a number is easier to compare than a shape.
results_table: Weight on day 1 (grams, if you have a scale)

materials.item: a cucumber, a tomato, a potato and a carrot
a piece of chapati, about the size of a slice
a knife and a chopping board
a steel plate or tray, and a thin clean cloth to cover it
a sheet of paper and a pencil to draw round each slice
a kitchen scale, if you have one (not needed)

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the slices with the knife. Do not eat the slices after drying, because they have sat out for days.

schedule.what: Cut five slices the same thickness. Guess which will shrink most. Draw round each one on paper. Weigh them if you have a scale. Put them by a sunny window, covered with a thin cloth.
Look at the slices. Turn them over so both sides dry.
Draw round each slice again, on top of the first outline. Weigh them again. Put them in order from most shrunk to least.

experiments.record: Draw each slice's outline on day 1 and again on day 3, one inside the other. If you weighed them, write both weights and how much each slice lost.

flow.do: 1. Cut one slice from each vegetable, about half a centimetre thick. 2. Cut a piece of chapati about the same size. 3. Lay all five on a sheet of paper and draw round each one with a pencil.
flow.say: All five slices start about the same size. Which one do you think will shrink the most when it dries? Why?
flow.kid: Draw round each slice on the paper. Which one will shrink the most? Put them in order. Say why.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: The cucumber feels wet, so it has lots of water.
The chapati is already dry, so it won't shrink much.

flow.context: This is the first step of the sun-dried slices test. You dry five foods for three days to find out how much of each is water.

flow.do: 1. If you have a kitchen scale, weigh each slice and write the number. 2. Move the slices onto the steel plate. 3. Cover with a thin cloth to keep flies off. 4. Put the plate by a sunny window or on a balcony.
flow.say: The cloth keeps flies off but lets air in. Sun and moving air help water leave the slices.
flow.kid: Weigh each slice if you have a scale. Put them on the plate. Cover them with a thin cloth. Put them in the sun.
flow.parent: A sunny window works in two or three days. In the monsoon, or in a dark flat, put the plate under a fan and give it an extra day. If a slice goes mouldy, throw it away and try again with a thinner slice in a sunnier spot.

flow.do: On day 2, look at the slices and turn each one over.
flow.say: What has changed since yesterday? Which slice has changed most?
flow.kid: Look at your slices. Turn each one over. Which one has changed most?

flow.do: 1. On day 3, lay each slice back on its outline and draw round it again. 2. Weigh them again if you have a scale. 3. Put them in order, from most shrunk to least.
flow.say: Where did the missing part of each slice go?
flow.kid: Put each slice on its first outline. Draw round it again. Which one shrank most? Where did the rest go?

check.q: The cucumber slice shrank to a thin, wrinkly disc. The chapati hardly changed size. What does this tell us?
options: The cucumber was mostly water, and the water went into the air
The chapati is stronger than the cucumber
check.why: A cucumber is nearly all water. The sun and moving air turned that water into water vapour, which went into the air. What is left is the small part of the cucumber that is not water: some sugar, fibre and minerals. Chapati is already much drier, so it had less water to lose. Picking 'the chapati is stronger' is a natural guess, but the difference is in how much water each food held.

flow.parent: With a scale, a cucumber slice of 20 grams usually ends at about 1 gram. A potato slice keeps about a fifth of its weight, because a potato is about four-fifths water and the rest is mostly starch. The tomato and carrot fall in between. A home scale that reads to 1 gram is good enough to see this.

experiments.context: In this three-day experiment you dry slices of four vegetables and a piece of chapati in the sun, to find out how much of each food is water.

experiments.title: Hidden Minerals: what is left when clear water dries?
experiments.question: Clear water looks empty. Does it leave anything behind when it dries?
experiments.predict: Look at five spoons of liquid that all look clear or nearly clear: filtered water, tap water, salt water, coconut water or sugar water, and whey. Which ones do you think will leave something on the plate when they dry? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same amount of each liquid, one teaspoon. Put them all on the same clean, dry steel plate, a hand-width apart. Dry them in the same place for the same time. Only the liquid changes. Filtered or RO water is the comparison.
results_table: My guess: will it leave something? (yes or no)
What was left (nothing, a faint ring, a white ring, crystals, a sticky film)

materials.item: a clean, dry steel plate (a dark plate or a black plastic lid shows white rings even better)
filtered or RO drinking water
tap water (borewell or corporation water, not filtered)
salt water: a pinch of salt stirred into 4 teaspoons of water
tender coconut water, or sugar water if you have no coconut
whey saved from the milk-splitting experiment (e1), if you have it
a teaspoon, paper slips and a pencil for labels

experiments.safety: Do not taste the spots. Wash the plate afterwards.

schedule.what: Guess which liquids will leave something behind. Put one teaspoon of each on the plate, labelled. Put it in the sun or under a fan.
Look at each dried spot closely, in good light. Fill in the table. Say what the spots tell you.

experiments.record: Draw the plate from above, with each spot and its label. Next to each spot, write what was left.

flow.do: 1. Wipe the steel plate clean and dry. 2. Put a paper label by each spot's place: filtered, tap, salt, coconut, whey. 3. Ask for a guess for each liquid.
flow.say: These liquids all look clear or nearly clear. Which ones do you think hide something inside? Why?
flow.kid: Label five places on the plate. Look at the five liquids. Which ones will leave something when they dry? Guess.

ask.q: Why do you think tap water will leave something, or not?
good: Our steel tumblers get white marks after we drink water.
Water is just water, so nothing will be left.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Hidden Minerals test. You dry spoons of clear liquids on a plate to see what they leave behind.

flow.do: 1. Put one teaspoon of each liquid on its place, a hand-width apart. 2. Put the plate flat in the sun or under a fan, where nobody will knock it.
flow.say: We use one teaspoon of each, so the test is fair. Now the water has to leave by itself.
flow.kid: Put one spoon of each liquid on its label. Do not let them touch. Put the plate in the sun.
flow.parent: In the sun, the spots dry in a few hours. Under a fan, leave them overnight.
flow.wait: Leave it until the spots are dry, a few hours or overnight.

flow.do: 1. Tilt the plate in good light. 2. Look closely at each spot. 3. Touch the coconut and whey spots with a finger. 4. Fill in the table.
flow.say: The water has gone into the air. What did each liquid leave behind?
flow.kid: Tilt the plate to the light. What is left of each spot? Touch the coconut and whey spots. Are they sticky?

check.q: The tap water left a white ring, but the filtered water left almost nothing. What is the white ring?
options: Minerals that were dissolved in the tap water
check.why: Tap water flows over and through rocks and soil, and picks up minerals like calcium. They dissolve, so you cannot see them. When the water dries, the minerals stay behind as a white ring. A filter or RO machine takes most of them out. Picking 'dust' is sensible, but dust would land on every spot equally. Picking 'soap' would also show on every spot, not only on tap water.

flow.parent: What you see depends on your water. Hard water, common from borewells in Chennai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad, leaves a clear white ring. Soft water may leave only a faint ring, so look closely. Salt water leaves small white crystals. Coconut water and whey leave a sticky, yellowish film: their sugars, with minerals mixed in.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think about clear water now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: clear water can carry minerals that I cannot see. What I saw: the tap water left a white ring and the filtered water left almost nothing. The whey left a sticky film. Why: minerals and sugar were dissolved in the water. When the water went into the air, they stayed on the plate. Your body gets some of its minerals from water in the same way.

experiments.context: In this experiment you dry spoons of clear liquids on a steel plate to find the minerals and sugars hidden in them.

activities.title: Ten-Spoon Foods: guess what a food is made of

materials.item: 10 spoons, or 10 bottle caps, or 10 dry chana
6 paper slips labelled water, carbohydrate, protein, fat, fibre, minerals
a cucumber, a glass of milk, a bowl of cooked rice, a spoon of dry toor dal and a few peanuts, to look at

the food card in this activity, for the parent: Food cards for the parent to read out, out of 10 spoons. Cucumber: 10 water (a tiny bit of sugar, fibre and minerals too). Milk: 9 water, 1 shared by milk sugar, fat, protein and minerals. Cooked rice: 7 water, 3 carbohydrate. Dry toor dal: 6 carbohydrate, 2 protein, 1 fibre, 1 water. Raw peanuts: 4 fat, 3 protein, 2 carbohydrate, 1 fibre and water.

activities.safety: Check for peanut allergy before handing out peanuts. Looking at them is enough.

schedule.what: Guess what each of five foods is made of, using 10 spoons. Then check against the food card.

activities.record: Draw a row of 10 circles for each food. Colour each circle for its nutrient: blue for water, yellow for carbohydrate, red for protein, orange for fat, green for fibre.

flow.do: 1. Lay the six paper slips in a row. 2. Put the cucumber and the 10 spoons in front of your child.
flow.say: Imagine we could take this cucumber apart into its nutrients, and fill 10 spoons. How many spoons would be water? How many carbohydrate, protein or fat? Put the spoons on the slips.
flow.kid: Imagine you take a cucumber apart into 10 spoons. Put the spoons on the slips. How many are water?
flow.context: This is the first step of Ten-Spoon Foods. You guess what five everyday foods are made of, and then find out.

flow.do: Read out the cucumber line from the food card. Let your child move the spoons to match. Ask if they are surprised.
flow.say: Scientists took cucumbers apart in a laboratory. Out of 10 spoons, all 10 are water, with a tiny bit of other things. Were you close?
flow.kid: Listen to the real answer. Move your spoons to match. Were you close?

flow.do: Do the same for milk, cooked rice, dry toor dal and peanuts. Guess first each time, then read the card.
flow.say: Now the dal. Most charts call dal a protein food. How many of the 10 spoons do you think are protein?
flow.kid: Now try milk, rice, dal and peanuts. Guess first. Then hear the answer.

check.q: Out of 10 spoons of dry toor dal, about how many are protein?
check.why: Only about 2 spoons out of 10 are protein. About 6 are carbohydrate. Dal is in the protein box because it has much more protein than rice or wheat, not because it is mostly protein. Picking 8 or 10 is what most people guess, because of the food group charts.

flow.parent: The big surprises are usually these. Milk is almost all water. Cooked rice is mostly water. Dal is mostly carbohydrate. Peanuts are more fat than protein. These numbers are rounded to the nearest spoon.

flow.do: Ask the question below and listen to the answer.
flow.say: We put dal in the protein box and peanuts in the protein box. Now that you know what is inside, is that fair? Why?
flow.kid: Is it fair to call dal a protein food? Say why or why not.
flow.parent: There is no single right answer. A good answer says that dal gives more protein than most plant foods, but most of it is carbohydrate. So a food group names only one part of a food.

activities.context: This is a quick guessing activity to start the unit. You guess what five foods are made of, using 10 spoons, and then hear what scientists found.

activities.title: The Breath Tumbler: find the water leaving your body

materials.item: a steel tumbler, cooled in the fridge for 10 minutes
a glass of drinking water

schedule.what: Breathe on a cold tumbler to see water leaving your body. List all the ways you lose and take in water.

activities.record: Draw yourself in the middle of a page. Draw arrows out for the ways water leaves you, and arrows in for the ways water comes in.

flow.do: 1. Take the cold tumbler out of the fridge. 2. Ask your child to breathe slowly onto the outside, from close up, three times.
flow.say: Breathe slowly onto the cold tumbler, three times. What appears? Where did it come from?
flow.kid: Breathe slowly onto the cold tumbler. Three times. What do you see on it?

ask.q: What is the mist on the tumbler?
good: Water vapour from inside me turned back into tiny drops on the cold steel.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Breath Tumbler. You find the water that leaves your body with every breath.

flow.do: Together, list every way water leaves the body and every way it comes in.
flow.say: Your breath carries water out. What other ways does water leave your body? And how does it come back in?
flow.kid: How else does water leave your body? How does it come back in? Make two lists.
flow.parent: Water leaves in breath, sweat, urine, tears and spit. It comes in from drinks, and from food like rasam, curd, fruit and vegetables. Your body also makes a little water when it burns food for energy.

flow.do: Ask your child to drink a glass of water slowly, and ask the question below.
flow.say: Water leaves you all day, even when you sit still. So what must you do all day too?
flow.kid: Drink a glass of water. Water leaves you all day. So what must you do?

check.q: Why do you need to drink water every day, even when you are not playing?
options: You lose water all day in your breath, sweat and urine
check.why: You lose water all day, even sitting still: in every breath, in sweat and in urine. So you must keep putting it back. Water has no energy in it, so picking 'energy' mixes water up with carbohydrates and fats.

activities.context: In this short activity you see water leaving your own body, and list how water goes out and comes in.

activities.title: My Body, Built from Food: a nutrient map

materials.item: a big sheet of paper, or old newspaper sheets taped together
crayons or colour pencils

schedule.what: Draw round your body on paper. Mark where each nutrient goes and what it does there.

activities.record: Keep your body map. Add a food next to each label that gives that nutrient.

flow.do: 1. Lay the paper on the floor. 2. Your child lies on it. 3. Draw round them with a crayon.
flow.say: Lie still while I draw round you. Then we'll mark what your body is built from.
flow.kid: Lie down on the paper. Keep still. A grown-up draws round you.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Body, Built from Food. You draw round your body and mark where each nutrient goes.

flow.do: Help your child draw and label these parts. Muscles: protein. Bones and teeth: calcium. Blood: iron and water. Eyes: vitamin A. Brain and running legs: carbohydrate for energy. A healing cut: vitamin C and protein.
flow.say: Your arm muscles are built from protein. Where does calcium go? What does your blood need? Let's draw them in.
flow.kid: Draw your bones, muscles, blood and eyes. Write which nutrient each one needs.

check.q: Which nutrient makes your bones and teeth hard?
check.why: Calcium is a mineral that makes bones and teeth hard. You get it from ragi, milk, curd, til and green leaves. Fat builds the skin of each cell, and vitamin C helps cuts heal.

flow.do: Next to each label, your child draws one food that gives that nutrient.
flow.say: Next to each label, draw one food from our kitchen that gives it.
flow.kid: Next to each label, draw one food that gives it.
flow.parent: Good choices: dal or curd for protein, ragi or milk for calcium, keerai for iron, carrot or mango for vitamin A, rice or idli for carbohydrate, coconut oil or peanuts for fat, amla or guava for vitamin C.

activities.context: In this activity you draw a life-size outline of your body and mark which nutrients build and run each part.

activities.title: Chana Sundal: cook a snack and find its nutrients

materials.item: white or black chana (kondakadalai), soaked overnight and pressure-cooked by a grown-up
grated coconut
1 teaspoon oil, a few mustard seeds, curry leaves, and salt
half a lemon
a kadai, a spoon and a bowl

activities.safety: A grown-up does the pressure-cooking and the tempering in hot oil. The child mixes the coconut, salt and lemon once the pan is off the flame.

schedule.what: Make chana sundal together. Name every ingredient's main nutrients. Eat it.

activities.record: Draw your bowl of sundal. Draw arrows from each ingredient to the nutrients it gives.

flow.do: 1. Heat 1 teaspoon of oil in the kadai. 2. Add mustard seeds and let them pop. 3. Add curry leaves and the cooked chana. 4. Stir for 2 minutes and turn off the flame.
flow.say: Sundal is made for Navaratri in many South Indian homes. Watch from a step back while the mustard seeds pop.
flow.kid: Watch the grown-up cook. Stand back when the mustard seeds pop.
flow.context: This is the first step of making chana sundal. You cook a simple snack and find the nutrients in each ingredient.

flow.do: Off the flame, your child adds the coconut, a pinch of salt and the lemon juice, and stirs.
flow.say: Now you add the last things. Coconut, a pinch of salt, and a squeeze of lemon.
flow.kid: Add the coconut, a pinch of salt and the lemon. Stir.

flow.do: Before eating, go through each ingredient and name its main nutrients together.
flow.say: Let's name what each part gives us. Chana? Coconut? Oil? Lemon? Salt?
flow.kid: Name what each part gives you. Chana. Coconut. Oil. Lemon. Salt.

check.q: In chana sundal, the chana gives protein, carbohydrate, fibre and iron. What does the squeeze of lemon add?
options: Vitamin C, which also helps your body take in the chana's iron
check.why: Lemon gives vitamin C. Vitamin C also helps the body take in iron from plant foods like chana. That is one reason a squeeze of lemon on dal or sundal is a good habit.

flow.parent: Chana: protein, carbohydrate, fibre, iron. Coconut: fat and fibre. Oil: fat. Lemon: vitamin C. Salt: the minerals sodium and, if iodised, iodine. Curry leaves: a little calcium and vitamin A. The cooking water in the chana is water too.

activities.context: In this cooking activity you make chana sundal, a South Indian snack, and name the nutrients that each ingredient brings.

projects.title: My Water Diary: three days of water in and out

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
your usual drinking tumbler, and a measuring cup or a 500 millilitre water bottle to measure it

projects.safety: Drink normally. This is a diary, not a contest to drink as much as possible.

schedule.what: Measure how much your tumbler holds. Make a tally chart. Tick each tumbler you drink, and each watery food you eat.
Keep ticking. Note the colour of your urine in the morning and the afternoon: pale, yellow or dark.
Finish the tally. Add up the millilitres. Compare a hot or busy day with a quiet one.

projects.record: A tally chart with three columns, one for each day. Count tumblers, watery foods (rasam, buttermilk, curd rice, fruit) and urine colour.

flow.do: 1. Fill a 500 millilitre bottle with water. 2. Pour it into the tumbler until full. 3. See how much is left in the bottle, and work out what the tumbler holds. 4. Draw a tally chart.
flow.say: First let's find out how much your tumbler holds. Then you can count tumblers and turn them into millilitres.
flow.kid: Find out how much your tumbler holds. Then draw a tally chart for three days.
flow.parent: Most steel tumblers hold between 150 and 250 millilitres. Write the number on the chart.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Water Diary, a 3-day project. You count how much water you take in and watch for signs that you need more.

flow.do: On day 2, keep ticking. Note the colour of urine in the morning and the afternoon.
flow.say: Pale yellow means your body has enough water. Dark yellow means it is asking for more.
flow.kid: Tick every tumbler. Check your urine colour. Pale is good. Dark means drink more.
flow.wait: Come back tomorrow and the day after.

flow.do: On day 3, add up each day's tumblers and turn them into millilitres. Talk about the differences.
flow.say: Which day did you drink most? Was it hotter, or did you play more?
flow.kid: Add up each day. Which day did you drink most? Why?

check.q: On the hot day you drank 2 more tumblers than on the cool day. Why does the body need more water on a hot day?
options: You sweat more, and sweat is mostly water
The Sun takes water out of the air you breathe
check.why: On a hot day your body sweats to cool you down. Sweat is mostly water, so you lose more and need to drink more. Watery foods like buttermilk and watermelon help too.

flow.parent: Many doctors suggest about 6 to 8 glasses of drinks a day for children, and more on hot days or after playing. Watery food counts too. Pale urine is a simpler guide than a number.

projects.context: In this 3-day project you keep a diary of the water you drink and eat, and learn to read your body's signs.
