challenges.title: Nothing Wasted: a plan for the whey
challenges.problem: When a family makes paneer from 1 litre of milk, about 800 millilitres of whey is left over. Most people pour it down the sink. Plan how your family could use all of it in one day, so the milk sugar, minerals and vitamins in it are not wasted.
constraints: Use only foods your family already cooks.
The whey must be used within a day, or kept in the fridge for up to two days.
Nobody should have to drink something they dislike.
materials: a look at what your family cooks in a week
whey from the milk-splitting experiment, if you have some
general: Knead chapati or poori dough with whey instead of water.
Cook rice or dal in whey instead of some of the water.
Use whey in place of water when making rasam.
creative: Use whey to soak the rice and urad dal for idli batter, and see if it changes the taste.
Water a potted plant with a little diluted whey, and compare with a plant given only water for two weeks.
Make a whey drink with a pinch of salt, roasted jeera and coriander, like neer mor.
challenges.your_turn: Write your plan for 800 millilitres of whey, with amounts for each use. Try one use this week and tell your family what nutrients the whey carried.

flow.do: Show your child the whey from the experiment, or remind them of it. Ask what is in it.
flow.say: Remember the pale liquid left when the milk split? What did it carry? Is it worth throwing away?
flow.kid: Remember the whey? What was in it? Should we throw it away?
flow.context: This is the first step of Nothing Wasted, a planning challenge. You plan how to use all the whey left from making paneer.

flow.do: Plan three or four uses together, with amounts that add up to 800 millilitres.
flow.say: How much whey would chapati dough for four people take? How much could go into the rasam?
flow.kid: Plan three uses for the whey. How much for each? Add them up to 800.
flow.parent: Chapati dough for four people takes about 200 to 300 millilitres of liquid. A pot of rasam takes about 500 millilitres. Whey is sour, so taste the dish before adding tamarind or lemon.

flow.do: Your child writes the plan and chooses one use to try.
flow.say: Which one shall we try this week? What do you think will happen to the taste?
flow.kid: Write your plan. Pick one to try this week.

check.q: Why is it worth using whey instead of throwing it away?
options: It still carries milk sugar, minerals, some vitamins and a little protein
It has most of the milk's fat
check.why: Whey is mostly water, but it also carries milk sugar, minerals, some vitamins and a little protein. Most of the fat stayed in the curds, with the casein.

challenges.context: This is a planning challenge. You design a way to use all the whey left from making paneer.

challenges.title: Sports Day Drink: keep the water and minerals in
challenges.problem: On a hot school sports day, children run for hours and sweat a lot. Sweat carries out water and some salt. Design a drink and a snack to carry, made at home, that puts back water, a little salt and some energy. No packaged drinks.
constraints: It must be made at home in 10 minutes.
It must stay safe to drink for a morning, in a bottle, without a fridge.
It must taste good enough that you actually drink it.
materials: salt, sugar, lemon, jaggery, buttermilk, jeera and tender coconut, from the kitchen
general: Nimbu pani: water, lemon juice, a little sugar and a pinch of salt.
Neer mor or sambharam: thin buttermilk with salt, curry leaves and ginger.
Tender coconut water, with a banana as the snack.
creative: Panakam, made for Rama Navami in many South Indian homes: water, jaggery, dry ginger, cardamom and a little lemon.
Freeze half the bottle overnight, then top it up in the morning, so it stays cool.
challenges.your_turn: Write the recipe for your drink and snack, and explain what each ingredient puts back. Make it before a busy, hot day, and see how you feel.

flow.do: Lick the back of your hand after playing hard, or remember how sweat tastes.
flow.say: Sweat tastes salty. So what does sweat carry out of your body, besides water?
flow.kid: Sweat tastes salty. What does it carry out of your body?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sports Day Drink challenge. You design a home-made drink that puts back what sweat takes out.

flow.do: Design one drink and one snack together. Name what each ingredient gives.
flow.say: Water puts back water. What puts back the salt? What gives energy for the next race?
flow.kid: Plan a drink and a snack. What does each part put back?
flow.parent: Water replaces water. A pinch of salt replaces some of the sodium lost in sweat. Sugar or jaggery gives quick energy, and also helps the gut take in salt and water. Doctors use a measured mix of salt and sugar in water, called ORS, for children who have lost a lot of water through diarrhoea.

flow.do: Make the drink. Taste it. Adjust.
flow.say: Taste it. Too salty? Too sweet? It should taste only lightly salty, a little less salty than tears.
flow.kid: Make your drink. Taste it. Change it until it tastes good.

check.q: Why does a sports day drink have a pinch of salt in it?
options: Sweat carries salt out of the body, so the salt puts some back
check.why: Sweat is mostly water, with a little salt. The salt is the mineral sodium chloride. A pinch in the drink puts some back. Salt has no energy in it, so energy has to come from sugar, jaggery or a snack.

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a drink and snack that put back the water, salt and energy you lose on a hot sports day.

quiz.p: How many kinds of nutrient does your body need?
opts: Six: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water
quiz.why: Scientists sort nutrients into six kinds. The body needs all of them.

quiz.p: Which nutrient does your body use most for energy?
quiz.why: Carbohydrates, like the starch in rice and idli, are the body's main fuel. Calcium builds bones, and vitamin C helps cuts heal.

quiz.p: Your hair, nails and muscles are made mostly of which nutrient?
quiz.why: Hair, nails and muscles are built mostly from protein. That is why growing children need protein every day.

quiz.p: Peanuts are in the protein group. Which other group could they also go in?
opts: Fats, because more than a third of a peanut is fat
quiz.why: A peanut has more fat than protein. So it fits the fats group as well. Most foods carry several nutrients.

quiz.p: Why can one food belong to more than one food group?
opts: Most foods are a mix of several nutrients
Cooks put foods in the wrong group
quiz.why: A food group names the nutrient a food gives most. But most foods carry several, so they can fit several groups.

quiz.p: Arjun, a boy of six, sees lemon juice make hot milk split. Which nutrients from the milk are mostly caught in the white lumps?
quiz.why: The lumps, called curds, hold most of the casein, the main protein in milk, with most of the fat caught inside. The watery whey holds most of the water, milk sugar and some minerals. Milk has no vitamin C to speak of.

quiz.p: Which of these would NOT make hot milk curdle?
quiz.why: Lemon juice and vinegar are acids, which make milk's protein clump. Sugar water is not an acid, so the milk stays smooth.

quiz.p: Why does a cucumber slice shrink so much when it dries in the sun?
opts: It is nearly all water, and the water goes into the air
quiz.why: A cucumber is nearly all water. When it dries, the water becomes water vapour in the air, and very little is left.

quiz.p: Which of these is a sign that your body needs more water?
quiz.why: Dark yellow urine means your body is keeping water back because it is short. Pale yellow usually means you have had enough.

quiz.p: Why can tap water leave a white ring on a steel tumbler?
opts: It carries dissolved minerals that stay behind when the water dries
The steel turns white when wet
quiz.why: Tap water picks up minerals like calcium from rocks and soil. They dissolve and cannot be seen. When the water dries, they stay as a white ring.

quiz.p: Which food gives a lot of calcium for strong bones?
quiz.why: Ragi is rich in calcium, a mineral that makes bones hard. Milk, curd, til and green leaves give calcium too.

quiz.p: In 1865, Fick and Wislicenus climbed a mountain to test an idea. What did they find?
opts: Muscles run mainly on carbohydrates and fats, not protein
quiz.why: They measured the nitrogen in their urine to see how much protein they used. It was far too little for the climb. So the energy came mostly from carbohydrates and fats.

quiz.p: How did Fick and Wislicenus measure how much protein their bodies used?
opts: They measured the nitrogen in their urine
They weighed themselves at the top
quiz.why: Protein is the nutrient with a lot of nitrogen. When the body breaks protein down, the nitrogen leaves in urine. So the nitrogen showed how much protein was used.

applications: Paneer, chhena for rasgulla, and cheese are all made by making milk's protein clump.
Doctors use blood tests to check iron, and give iron tablets to children who are short of it.
India adds iodine to most salt, which has greatly reduced goitre, a swelling in the neck.
ORS, a measured mix of salt and sugar in water, saves the lives of many children with diarrhoea.
School midday meals in India are planned so that children get enough protein and energy.
Food scientists measure the nutrients in foods so that packet labels can list them.
Water filters and RO machines take minerals out of hard water.
Athletes plan their carbohydrates before a long race, because muscles run mainly on them.

open_questions.q: Exactly how much protein does a growing child need?
open_questions.why_open: Different countries set slightly different numbers, and scientists still study how growth, activity and food mixes change the need.

open_questions.q: Are ghee and coconut oil good or bad for the heart?
open_questions.why_open: Studies disagree. Some find they raise harmful fats in the blood, others find little effect when the whole diet is healthy.

open_questions.q: Why does life use so many different vitamins?
open_questions.why_open: We know what many vitamins do, but not why living things came to need so many different small helpers.

open_questions.q: How much of the protein in a meal does each person really take in?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on the food, the cooking, the person's gut and their microbes. Scientists are still measuring this for many Indian foods.

open_questions.q: Are there nutrients we have not found yet?
open_questions.why_open: The last vitamin was named in 1948. Scientists still find substances in food that seem to help the body, and argue about whether to call them nutrients.

maths.problem: In Ten-Spoon Foods, dry toor dal is about 2 spoons of protein out of 10. What fraction of the dal is protein? Write it two ways.
maths.answer: 2 out of 10, which is the same as 1 out of 5.
maths.explain: 2 spoons out of 10 is two-tenths. If you put the 10 spoons into 5 equal groups of 2, the protein fills 1 group. So it is also one-fifth.
maths.context: In Ten-Spoon Foods, you split everyday foods into 10 spoons, one for each tenth of the food.
maths.why_maths: Fractions let us say how much of a food is protein, whatever the size of the bowl.

maths.problem: Kavya split 200 millilitres of milk with 20 millilitres of lemon juice. She collected 180 millilitres of whey. About how much went into the curds?
maths.explain: She started with 200 + 20 = 220 millilitres of liquid. 180 millilitres came out as whey. 220 - 180 = 40. So about 40 millilitres went into the curds. That is much less than the whey.
maths.context: In the milk-splitting experiment, lemon juice splits hot milk into curds and whey.
maths.why_maths: Taking away what came out from what went in tells us how much stayed in the curds, without having to measure them.

maths.problem: A cucumber slice weighed 20 grams and dried to 1 gram. A potato slice weighed 20 grams and dried to 4 grams. How much water did each lose? Which food had more that was not water?
maths.answer: The cucumber lost 19 grams. The potato lost 16 grams. The potato had more that was not water: 4 grams instead of 1.
maths.explain: 20 - 1 = 19 grams of water from the cucumber. 20 - 4 = 16 grams from the potato. What is left is the part that is not water. 4 grams is 4 times as much as 1 gram.
maths.context: In the sun-dried slices test, you dry slices of vegetables for three days to find their water.
maths.why_maths: Weighing before and after turns 'it shrank a lot' into a number we can compare between foods.

maths.problem: Meena's steel tumbler holds 200 millilitres. On Monday she drank 6 tumblers. On Tuesday, a hot sports day, she drank 9. How much more did she drink on Tuesday, in millilitres? Why might that be?
maths.answer: 600 millilitres more. On a hot sports day she sweated more, so she needed more water.
maths.explain: Monday: 6 x 200 = 1,200 millilitres. Tuesday: 9 x 200 = 1,800 millilitres. 1,800 - 1,200 = 600. That is 3 more tumblers, because sweat carries water out of the body.
maths.context: In My Water Diary, you count the tumblers you drink each day for three days.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups of 200 turns tumblers into millilitres, so two days can be compared fairly.

maths.problem: 100 grams of ragi flour has about 340 milligrams of calcium. 100 millilitres of milk has about 120 milligrams. Is the ragi's calcium closer to 2 times or 3 times the milk's?
maths.explain: 2 x 120 = 240, and 3 x 120 = 360. 340 is much closer to 360 than to 240. So ragi has nearly 3 times as much calcium as the same amount of milk.
maths.context: This compares the calcium, a mineral for strong bones, in ragi and in milk.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'nearly 3 times as much' is easier to remember and compare than two big numbers.

maths.problem: In Two-Box Foods, Arjun found a second box for 8 of the 20 food cards. Kavya found a second box for 12. Make a tally chart for both and say what the numbers suggest about food groups.
maths.answer: Arjun: 8 tallies. Kavya: 12 tallies. More than a third of the foods fit two boxes for both players, so many foods are a mix of nutrients.
maths.explain: Tally in groups of five: Arjun has one group of 5 and 3 more. Kavya has two groups of 5 and 2 more. 8 and 12 are both more than a third of 20, which is about 7. So many foods belong in two boxes.
maths.context: In Two-Box Foods, you score extra for finding a second food group for a food.
maths.why_maths: A tally makes it easy to count and compare, and the count shows how common two-box foods are.

roots.context: We have learned that food is made of six kinds of nutrient, and that most foods carry several at once. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Lemon juice split your hot milk into white curds and pale, watery whey. The curds held most of the protein and fat. The whey kept the water, the milk sugar and some minerals. So one glass of milk carries many nutrients, and its food group names only one of them.
deep_truth.habit: We sort foods into boxes: dal is 'protein', rice is 'carbohydrate', milk is 'dairy'. The box makes each food sound like one thing. But a box is a label for planning meals, and most foods are mixes that the label leaves out.
deep_truth.evidence: In the milk-splitting test, lemon juice split milk into curds and much more whey. Dried on a plate, the whey left a sticky film of milk sugar and minerals. Measured in a laboratory, dry toor dal is about one-fifth protein and more than half carbohydrate.

roots.thread: Sugar, starch, fat and protein look and taste very different. Yet all of them are built mostly from three kinds of atoms: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with nitrogen added in protein. Joined one way, these atoms make sweet sugar. Joined another way, they make oil, or the white curds of paneer. Inside you, they are taken apart and joined again into muscle, blood and the skin of your cells. A few kinds of atoms, joined in many ways, make every food and every body.

teachings.teaching: Food, when eaten, is divided into three. Its coarsest part becomes waste. Its middle part becomes flesh. Its finest part becomes mind.
teachings.link: The sage saw that food splits into parts with different jobs. Science sorts the parts differently, into nutrients, but it also finds that each part of a food goes to a different use in the body.

teachings.link: Sugar, fat and protein are made from the same few kinds of atoms. How the atoms are joined decides whether you get sweet sugar or paneer.

science.text: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are built mostly from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms. Proteins also contain nitrogen.
The body takes the proteins in food apart into amino acids, and builds its own proteins from them.
Exactly how much protein a growing child needs is still studied, and countries set slightly different numbers.

other_view.view: Food groups are a useful shortcut, not a mistake. A parent planning a meal needs a quick rule, not a chemistry table. Calling dal a protein food is fair, because for vegetarian families it is one of the best sources of protein.

Splitting Milk (e1): 1 tablespoon of lemon juice in half a cup of milk heated until steaming curdles it within a minute or two, which is more acid per cup than a usual paneer recipe, so the result is clear. Cold milk curdles slowly with tiny lumps, so the milk is heated by a grown-up and the step says what to do if the lumps are small. Vinegar is optional, with sour curd as a swap. how_we_found_out.story: In the 1840s, Justus von Liebig, a famous German chemist, taught that working muscles burn up their own protein. So people thought protein foods were the main fuel for hard work. In 1865 two professors in Zurich, Adolf Fick and Johannes Wislicenus, decided to test this on themselves. Protein is the only nutrient in food with a lot of nitrogen in it. When the body breaks protein down, that nitrogen leaves in urine. So by measuring the nitrogen in their urine, they could work out how much protein their bodies had used. In August 1865 they climbed the Faulhorn, a mountain in Switzerland, nearly 2,000 metres up from the lake below. Before and during the climb they ate no protein, only food made of starch, fat and sugar. They collected their urine and measured its nitrogen. The protein they had used could give only a small part of the energy needed to lift their bodies up the mountain. The rest of the energy had to come from starch, fat and sugar. Liebig was wrong. Muscles run mainly on carbohydrates and fats. Protein is used mostly to build and mend the body.
how_we_found_out.who: Adolf Fick, a physiologist, and Johannes Wislicenus, a chemist, both professors in Zurich
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Justus von Liebig taught that working muscles burn their own protein, so protein is the main fuel for work. The Faulhorn climb showed that protein gave only a small part of the energy. Most of it came from carbohydrates and fats.
